title: Biological Physics
text:
FYS3715 · Spring 2027 · University of Oslo
    How does a bacterium find food in a world without inertia? Why does a cell burst in pure water?
       How can entropy create order? And how do identical cells organise themselves into a tissue with a shape?
In this course you use statistical physics, soft matter and mechanics to build quantitative models of living systems on scales from 1 nm to a few hundred micrometres. You test the models against your own measurements and simulations.

title: 3D: Orientation order in epithelial monolayers, towards a paper
text:
Over the last decade, many papers have reported nematic order in layers of epithelial cells: regions where the elongated cells align, with topological defects between them, analysed with the theory of active liquid crystals. Most of these claims rest on still images, and few compare the measured order with what a random layer would give. In 2025, two students in this course, Giulio Simonetti and Tobit Roth, built a full analysis pipeline for our quantitative phase movies of MDCK monolayers, from scratch. We have started a manuscript from it, with them as co-authors. What is missing is the part that decides what can be claimed:

Is there nematic order in MDCK monolayers that is stronger, larger or longer-lived than chance? At which densities, length scales and time scales?

This is a research project with an open answer. It continues 2C Active cell layers: if you did 2C you already have the tools; if not, the first week brings you up to speed. If the results are good, they go into the paper, and students who contribute substantially are offered co-authorship too.

title: 3D: Orientation order in epithelial monolayers, towards a paper
text:
What exists

Time-lapse quantitative phase (Holomonitor) movies of MDCK monolayers from five experiments in 2024: freely expanding layers and layers confined on circular islands, 110–337 frames each, at a range of densities. The pixel values are cell heights.
A Python package by Simonetti and Roth (segmentation, cell shapes and orientations, coarse-grained nematic fields, ±½ defect detection), extended in 2026 with pixel-resolution fields and frame-to-frame defect matching. Four notebooks take you from raw images to defect statistics.
A manuscript draft, Persistence of elongation and orientation in MDCK monolayers, with the methods written and the results section planned in four parts: aspect-ratio distributions, the lifetime of cell orientation, nematic order against coarse-graining scale, and defect dynamics.

Data, code and notebooks are in one repository on UiO’s GitHub (github.uio.no/dagkd/orient_mdck), with five movies ready to analyse. Its README explains how to start. You get access, and access to the manuscript, at the kick-off.

title: 3D: Orientation order in epithelial monolayers, towards a paper
section: Choose one part of the paper
text:
Choose one part of the paper
Each part is a project in itself. With two or three students, each takes a different part.
A. Cell shape: is the aspect-ratio distribution universal? Sadhukhan and Nandi (eLife 2022) predict a one-parameter distribution of cell aspect ratios for confluent layers. Measure the distributions for all data sets, test the predicted data collapse and the relation between the spread and the mean, and find how the parameter depends on cell density. Which physical quantity does it correspond to?
B. How long do cells keep their shape and orientation? Track individual cells from frame to frame and measure the autocorrelation times of their area, height, aspect ratio and orientation. Are shapes and orientations short-lived compared with other processes in the layer, such as the 2–4 hour height pulsations we see? If an orientation lasts only minutes, can it matter biologically?
C. Nematic order against length and time scale. Measure the coarse-grained order parameter \(S(R)\) and the orientation correlation function against distance and time lag. Compare each with a null model at every scale. Over what range, if any, is there order beyond chance, and how does it depend on density?
D. Are the defects real? Measure the density, lifetime and motion of ±½ defects against the coarse-graining radius. Do the same for orientation fields from the null model. Real defects should live longer, and move differently, than the defects that noise alone creates.

title: 3D: Orientation order in epithelial monolayers, towards a paper
section: Validation: what makes a result publishable
text:
Validation: what makes a result publishable

A null model for every statistic. Keep the positions and shapes of the cells but shuffle their orientations (within a frame, and between frames). Also compute the finite-sample baseline: with \(n\) cells in a window, random orientations give \(S\approx\sqrt{\pi/(4n)}\). A result counts only where it lies clearly outside the null distribution. In a related project on gastruloids, this test removed most of the long-range order that had first been reported.
A test on known data. Apply exactly the same pipeline to simulated orientation fields with a known correlation length (or to Vicsek simulations at high and low noise, as in 2C). The pipeline must find the order you put in, and none where there is none.
Robustness to segmentation. Rerun your main result with different segmentation parameters, and on a manually checked region. A result that changes when the segmentation changes is a result about the segmentation.

title: 2B: Nerve signals, from Nernst to Hodgkin–Huxley
text:
Every animal cell has a voltage across its membrane, but nerve cells use it to send signals: a sharp pulse, the action potential, travels along the axon at constant speed and shape. In the brain, neuroscientists often see these pulses only indirectly, as flashes of fluorescence from calcium that enters the cell when it fires. Your question is:

How do ion gradients and voltage-gated channels produce an action potential, and what can a calcium signal tell us about how a neuron fires?

The physics is from Block B: the Nernst potential, ion pumps and the resting potential (Membrane potentials and ion pumps), and then Nelson chapter 12. The simulation exercise was written by Geir Halnes (NMBU) and has been used in the course since 2019.



Calcium imaging: a single action potential, evoked by current injection, raises the intracellular calcium concentration by 50–100 nM, which then decays back to baseline (from Rudolph, Hull and Regehr, J. Neurosci. 2015).

title: 2B: Nerve signals, from Nernst to Hodgkin–Huxley
text:
What the project should contain

1. The resting potential (weeks 11–13)
Write a small time-dependent model of a cell with Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻ channels (Ohmic leaks, see the notes), a 3:2 sodium–potassium pump and trapped macroions. Let the concentrations and the potential evolve from an initial state to steady state.

Show that the steady state reproduces the analytical pump–leak potential, and that chloride ends up at its Nernst potential.
What happens when you switch the pump off? How long does it take for the cell to run down, and towards what state?



2. The action potential (from week 14)
Work through Problems 1 and 2 of the notebook: speed up the gating rates to brain temperature, find the firing rate against input current (the \(f\)–\(I\) curve) and its threshold, and add a high-voltage-activated calcium channel.


3. Calcium dynamics and the data
Work through Problem 3 of the notebook: add intracellular calcium, and tune its parameters to the experiment. Then analyse the imaging data in ca_imaging_mean_intensity.csv:

Find the individual calcium transients, subtract the background and fit their decay. What is the decay time, and how does it compare with \(\tau_\text{Ca}\) in the model?
What can and cannot be inferred about the firing rate from the rise of the fluorescence?



4. Validation

Check the Nernst potentials in the model by hand from the concentrations.
Show that the model converges: halve the time step and compare.
Without calcium, the original model must fire two action potentials for the default stimulus (as stated in the notebook). Check it before changing anything.
For a single spike, the calcium rise should equal \(k_\text{Ca}\) times the integrated calcium current, and the decay should be exponential with time constant \(\tau_\text{Ca}\). Check both against your simulation.

title: E7: Depletion forces and osmotic pressure
section: 2. Molar mass from osmotic pressure, and oedema
text:
2. Molar mass from osmotic pressure, and oedema

The osmotic pressure of the proteins in blood plasma at body temperature (take 303 K) is about 28 mm Hg (752 mm Hg = \(1.01\times10^5\) Pa). The plasma contains about 60 g/L of protein. Assuming a dilute solution, estimate the average molar mass of the plasma proteins (Nelson, Problem 7.4).
The capillary walls let water through: a pressure difference \(\Delta P\) across them drives a volume flux (volume per area per time) \(L_p\Delta P\), with \(L_p = 7\times10^{-6}\) cm s⁻¹ atm⁻¹. Normally the osmotic pressure of the plasma proteins roughly balances other forces across the capillaries. In an undernourished person, the plasma proteins are reduced by 10 %. How much fluid accumulates outside the capillaries per day, if their total open area is about 250 m²? Why do starving children get swollen bellies?

title: E7: Depletion forces and osmotic pressure

3. Depletion forces in the cell
A typical globular protein is a sphere of radius about 10 nm. Suppose such proteins fill about 30 % of the cytoplasm (Nelson, Problem 7.5).

Two large, flat macromolecular complexes with matching surfaces approach each other face to face. Draw the depletion zones and estimate the separation at which a depletion force begins to act.
The contact area is 10 µm². Estimate the free energy gained when the surfaces stick, using the van ’t Hoff relation for the osmotic pressure of the proteins. Compare with \(k_BT\).
Is the van ’t Hoff relation a good approximation here? Would the real depletion attraction be stronger or weaker?

title: Lab: Brownian motion
text: The purpose of this lab is to learn some basic statistical physics, microscopy, imaging and image analysis. The data you take here are the data for Project 1. The theory is in the notes on active and passive motion, sections on random walks, diffusion, viscous drag and the Langevin equation.

title: Lab: Brownian motion
text:
Background

Nobel Prize in 2009
Electronic cameras surround us everywhere and have been used scientifically since they were invented. In 2009, Willard S. Boyle and George E. Smith at Bell Laboratories were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics “for the invention of an imaging semiconductor circuit, the CCD sensor”.


The optical microscope
The microscope is a stable stand that allows small, controlled movements of what you are looking at relative to the light source and the objective. The illumination is at least as important for what you see as the type of objective you use. If the illumination is correct, the resolution of the microscope is set by the numerical aperture (NA) of the objective. The resolution is the radius of the diffraction pattern from point sources, and is at best \(r=\lambda/(2\,\mathrm{NA})\), where \(\lambda\) is the wavelength of the light. We have two objectives with NA = 0.4 and NA = 0.65, so the resolutions for green light are \(D_{20X}=0.7\) µm and \(D_{40X}=0.4\) µm.


Imaging with electronic cameras
The objective sends out an almost parallel beam of rays. This beam must pass through an eyepiece to form an image on the retina, or through an imaging lens to form an image on the sensor of a camera. In an electronic camera, electrons are released where light falls on a semiconductor chip. The chip is divided into many pixels, each of which works as a light sensor.

The spatial resolution of a camera is set by how many pixels the chip is divided into.
Just as important is the intensity resolution: how many intensity levels each pixel can distinguish. It depends on the pixel size (larger pixels collect more electrons), the sensor temperature (fewer thermal noise electrons when cold) and the readout noise (usually larger for faster readout). Most simple cameras and image formats use \(2^8=256\) levels (8 bit). Good SLR cameras have a raw format with 12 bit (\(2^{12}=4096\) levels). Good scientific cameras are cooled to between −80 and −180 °C and have expensive readout electronics giving \(2^{16}=65536\) levels. Then each pixel is an accurate, sensitive light meter.
Square pixels are an advantage: the conversion from pixels to object size is then the same horizontally and vertically.
If you do not need colour information, a greyscale camera is better, because colour filtering costs both spatial and intensity resolution.
The last choice is the chip technology, CCD or CMOS.



Image analysis






Figure 1: Analysis of an imaged square grid. Top left: monochrome image of a square grid with 50 µm between the lines and 5 µm wide lines. Top right: the same image as a matrix \(I\), shown as a colour map. Note that the element \(I[0,0]\) is in the upper left corner. Bottom: vertical cross-section I[:, 500] on the left and horizontal cross-section I[500, :] on the right.



We only use monochrome cameras here. A monochrome image is a 2D matrix with elements \(I_{ij}\), \(i=1\ldots N_y\), \(j=1\ldots N_x\). For an 8-bit image, \(I_{ij}\) is between 0 (black) and 255 (white). The pixel coordinates correspond to object coordinates \(x_j=j s_x\) and \(y_i=i s_y\), where \(s_x\) and \(s_y\) are the pixel sizes in the object (µm per pixel). One of the first things to do with a new imaging system is to find \(s_x\) and \(s_y\) by imaging an object of known size and counting how many pixels it covers.
Figure 1 shows a greyscale image with 1024 × 1280 pixels and intensities between 50 and 240. The positions of the horizontal lines are the 4 minima in the lower left plot, and the positions of the vertical lines are the 5 minima in the lower right plot. Since the lines are 50 µm apart, these minima give \(s_x\) and \(s_y\).
In Python:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pims

I = pims.as_gray(pims.open('grid20x.png'))[0]  # greyscale matrix
plt.imshow(I, cmap='gray'); plt.colorbar()
plt.figure(); plt.plot(I[:, 500]); plt.plot(I[500, :])
trackpy does not read images itself. It uses PIMS, which we use here too, so the calibration image and the movie are read the same way. pims.open reads a single image, a folder of images ('stack/*.png') or a video file, and returns a list of frames. pims.as_gray converts colour frames to greyscale and leaves greyscale frames as they are.

title: Lab: Brownian motion
text:

text:
In the lab

Imaging quality and calibration
Get help to place the test slide in the microscope, turn on the light, open the camera program, and set the camera to take pictures continuously and show them on the screen. Never touch the surface of the test slide!

Use the 20X objective, find a field with a square grid, and focus while looking in the eyepiece.
Open a window that shows the histogram and a window where you can set the exposure time. The histogram shows how many pixels have each intensity. You should see two peaks, one for the white stripes and one for the black stripes.
Set a light intensity that is comfortable for the eyes. Then adjust the focus and the exposure time to get the largest possible distance between the two peaks in the histogram. You now have maximum contrast.
Save a still image of the grid and determine \(s_x\) and \(s_y\) as in Figure 1.
Repeat for the 40X objective.
Is the resolution limited by diffraction or by the camera pixels? Calculate \(D_{20X}/s_x\) and \(D_{40X}/s_x\) and explain what these ratios tell you.
Optional: Modulation transfer function (MTF). With the 20X objective, focus on the field with 60 LP/mm (line pairs per millimetre) and optimise contrast. Save an image, plot an intensity profile normal to the stripes, and note \(I_{\min}\) and \(I_{\max}\). Repeat with 380, 500 and 600 LP/mm, and then with the 40X objective. Plot \(\mathrm{MTF}(f)=(I_{\max}(f)-I_{\min}(f))/(I_{\max}(60)-I_{\min}(60))\) for both objectives.



Brownian motion
Get help from a supervisor to prepare a microscope slide with a small volume of liquid containing small particles. Use the 20X objective and normal illumination to find an area with particles. Switch to dark-field illumination if it is difficult to find the particles.

Take one picture of the particles with normal illumination and one with dark-field illumination, with the best contrast you can get. Describe the difference between the two images and how each is produced.
Determine the mean particle size in pixels and in micrometres. Compare with the nominal bead size and with the resolution of the objective.
Record a 30 s movie at 15 frames per second with the best contrast and focus. Play it a few times (e.g. in ImageJ/Fiji) to see roughly how far the most mobile particles move during the movie.

Record a 5 min movie at 15 frames per second with the best possible contrast and focus.
Write down: objective, pixel size, frame rate, exposure time, bead size (nominal), temperature in the room, and anything that may cause drift (evaporation, a tilted stage, a warm lamp).

title: 2A: Freezing cells, the physics of cryopreservation
text:
Almost every life-science lab keeps cells in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C, and thaws them again to use them. Many cells do not survive. When ice forms inside a cell, it is almost always fatal. The standard way to avoid that is to cool slowly, so that ice forms outside first and pulls water out of the cell by osmosis. But a cell that loses too much water sits for a long time in concentrated salt, which also kills it. Your question is:

Why is there an optimal cooling rate for freezing cells, and what sets it?

title: 2A: Freezing cells, the physics of cryopreservation
text:
Almost every life-science lab keeps cells in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C, and thaws them again to use them. Many cells do not survive. When ice forms inside a cell, it is almost always fatal. The standard way to avoid that is to cool slowly, so that ice forms outside first and pulls water out of the cell by osmosis. But a cell that loses too much water sits for a long time in concentrated salt, which also kills it. Your question is:

Why is there an optimal cooling rate for freezing cells, and what sets it?

The physics is from Block B: the chemical potential of water and ice, osmosis, freezing point depression and water permeation through the membrane (Processes at membranes, E8). Background reading: A. title: 2A: Freezing cells, the physics of cryopreservation
text:
What the project should contain

1. Equilibrium: how much water does ice pull out?

Use the Gibbs free energy of water and ice to show that below the melting point \(T_m\) their chemical potentials differ by \(\Delta\mu\approx -\Delta h_m\,\Delta T/T_m\) per molecule, where \(\Delta h_m\) is the latent heat of melting per molecule and \(\Delta T = T - T_m < 0\).
Use the Gibbs–Duhem relation to find the solute concentration of a liquid in equilibrium with ice at temperature \(T\), the freezing point depression. What is the freezing point of a cell at physiological osmolarity (300 mM)?
Combine with the Boyle–van ’t Hoff relation (E8) to get the equilibrium cell volume against temperature down to −40 °C. Where does the dilute-solution theory stop being trustworthy?



2. Kinetics: how fast can water leave?
Water leaves through the membrane with a volume flux proportional to the osmotic imbalance. For a cell of area \(A\) and water volume \(W\),
\[
\frac{dW}{dt} = -A\,P_f\,v_w\left[c_\text{out}(T) - c_\text{in}(W)\right],
\]
where \(P_f\) is the osmotic water permeability, \(v_w\) the molar volume of water, \(c_\text{out}(T)\) the concentration of the unfrozen solution outside (set by the ice) and \(c_\text{in}\) the concentration inside. \(P_f\) falls steeply with temperature, typically with an Arrhenius law with an activation energy of tens of kJ/mol.

Derive the time constant for the cell to adjust its volume. For a cell of radius 10 µm, what is it at room temperature and at −10 °C?
Solve the equation for cooling at a constant rate \(B\) (from 0.1 to 1000 K/min) and plot the cell volume against temperature.
The intracellular solution is supercooled by the difference between its own freezing point and \(T\). Plot the supercooling against temperature for each rate.

Choose parameter values for one real cell type (for example a mouse oocyte, a red blood cell or a stem cell) from the literature. Give your sources, and say which numbers you are least sure of.


3. Validation

Slow limit. For \(B\to0\) the volume must follow the equilibrium curve from part 1. Show that it does.
Fast limit. For \(B\to\infty\) the cell has no time to lose water. Its volume must stay at the initial value, and the supercooling must equal the full \(T_m - T\) minus the freezing point depression.
Numerics. Show that your result does not change when you halve the time step or tighten the solver tolerance.



4. The optimal cooling rate
Use your results to explain the “two-factor hypothesis”: slow cooling kills by long exposure to concentrated solution, fast cooling by intracellular ice. Define a criterion for each kind of damage (for example, a maximum tolerated supercooling and a maximum time above a given concentration), and find the cooling rate between them. How does the optimum depend on cell size and on \(P_f\)? Compare with cooling rates used in practice (about 1 K/min for many mammalian cells).


Possible wet-lab addition (Tue 13 Apr, to be confirmed)
Measure the volume of cells in solutions of different osmolarity in the microscope, and make a Boyle–van ’t Hoff plot to find the osmotically inactive volume of your cells. Use it in your model.

title: 2C: Active cell layers, from Vicsek to epithelia
text:
Epithelial cells, the cells that line our organs, form dense layers in which they push, crawl and align with their neighbours. Physicists describe such layers as active matter, the same class as the flocks of the Vicsek model. Images of real cell layers often seem to show regions of aligned cells. But a pattern that looks ordered to the eye can also arise by chance. Your question is:

Do the cells in an epithelial monolayer align with each other, beyond what chance would give?

You will first map the order–disorder transition in the Vicsek model, where you know the answer, and use it to build and test your tools. Then you apply the same tools to quantitative phase images of MDCK epithelial monolayers from our group.

title: 2C: Active cell layers, from Vicsek to epithelia
text:
What the project should contain

1. The flocking transition

Run the Vicsek model for a grid of noise amplitudes \(\eta\) and densities \(\rho = Nr^2/L^2\). Plot the polar order parameter \(\varphi = \left|\frac1N\sum_j e^{i\theta_j}\right|\) in the steady state against \(\eta\) for each density.
How do you know the simulation has reached a steady state? How large are the fluctuations of \(\varphi\)?
Finite-size check. For fully random orientations, \(\varphi\) is not zero but of order \(1/\sqrt N\). Show this, and use it to decide when a measured \(\varphi\) means order.



2. Cell shape and orientation in the monolayer

Segment the cells with the notebook. Check the segmentation by eye on a part of the image, and estimate how often it splits or merges cells.
For each cell, compute the area, the aspect ratio and the orientation of the long axis from the second moments of its shape. Cell orientation is a nematic quantity: a cell pointing at \(\theta\) is the same as one pointing at \(\theta + \pi\).
Plot the distributions of area and aspect ratio, and how they change with cell density.



3. Is there nematic order?

Define the nematic order parameter in a window of radius \(R\), \(S(R) = \left|\langle e^{2i\theta_j}\rangle_{j\in R}\right|\), averaged over many windows, and plot it against \(R\).
Null model. Keep the positions and shapes of the cells, but shuffle the orientations randomly between cells. Repeat many times to get the distribution of \(S(R)\) for a layer with no correlations. With \(n\) cells in a window, a random layer gives \(S\approx\sqrt{\pi/(4n)}\). Is the measured \(S(R)\) outside the null distribution? At which \(R\)?
Test on known data. Before you trust part 3 on cells, apply exactly the same analysis to a Vicsek simulation (use \(e^{2i\theta}\) of the particle directions) at low and at high noise. The method must find order where there is order, and none where there is none.



4. Discussion
What does your result say about whether an epithelial layer behaves like a Vicsek flock? What would you need to measure to tell them apart: polar or nematic order, motion or shape?

title: Working with LLMs
text: In this course you are expected to use large language models (LLMs) such as GPT UiO: for setting up Python, writing and debugging analysis code, understanding methods, and writing reports. This is how much research and technical work is done today. What the course assesses is your own understanding, and that is checked in the oral defenses and the final exam.

title: Working with LLMs
section: What an LLM is good and bad at here
text:
What an LLM is good and bad at here
Good at: installing packages and fixing error messages, writing first versions of analysis code, explaining what a function or a parameter does, suggesting how to plot or fit something, and turning your notes into readable text.
Bad at: knowing what your data look like, knowing whether a number is physically reasonable, and noticing when code runs but gives the wrong answer. It will often answer confidently when it is wrong.

title: Working with LLMs
text:
Five habits

Give it the physics and the numbers. “Beads of 0.51 µm, 0.1837 µm per pixel, 15 fps, I expect D ≈ 0.9 µm²/s” gets you far better help than “how do I use trackpy?”.
Ask it to explain, not only to write. For every step, ask why. If you cannot explain a line of your code, you do not yet own it.
Test on data with a known answer. Synthetic data, a limiting case, a simple estimate. If the method fails there, it fails on your data too.
Estimate before you compute. Know the order of magnitude you expect before you look at the result.
Keep a log. Note what you asked, what went wrong and how you found out. It becomes the LLM log in your report and good material for the defense.

The LLM log in your reports
One page appended to each report:

What you used an LLM for (code, debugging, explanations, writing).
At least one example where it was wrong, misleading or incomplete, and how you found out.
What you checked yourself, and how.

The log is not graded on how much or how little you used an LLM. It shows that you know where the result comes from.
